one_liner: C++20 fork of cereal with a buffered binary archive: 1.3-2.1x faster than cereal, 1.1-2.8x than Boost, on small-field data.
what_it_does: A near source-compatible C++20 rewrite of cereal. You write the same serialize/save/load (and save_minimal/load_minimal) functions, call archive(x, y, z), and get binary, portable-binary, JSON and XML archives with support for std containers, smart pointers, polymorphic types and class versioning. Moving from cereal is mostly a rename of the namespace (cereal:: to ser20::) and the macro prefix (SER20_REGISTER_TYPE and so on). SFINAE dispatch is replaced with C++20 requires-clauses, and there is an experimental C++20 module interface (module/ser20.cppm). Unlike cereal, it is not header-only: two .cpp files (shared-pointer storage and the polymorphic caster registry) must be compiled.
how_it_is_fast: cereal's BinaryArchive makes one streambuf sputn/sgetn call per primitive, so a vector of structs or a container of short strings pays that per-call stream overhead for every field. ser20's BinaryOutputArchive memcpys writes under 1 KiB into a 4 KiB buffer and flushes it at the end of each top-level archive call; this is write coalescing. BinaryInputArchive reads the stream in 4 KiB chunks and serves small loads from that buffer (read-ahead buffering). Dispatch functions are also marked always_inline + nodebug (SER20_HIDE_FUNCTION). Contiguous arithmetic vectors and single large strings already go out as one bulk write in both libraries, so they gain nothing.
when_to_use: An existing cereal codebase on BinaryArchive where profiles show time in many small field writes: vectors of structs, map<string, struct>, many short strings. The repo's numbers show 1.8-2.1x faster saves and 1.3-1.8x faster loads than cereal on these.

Moving off boost::serialization to a cereal-style API. ser20 keeps cereal's Boost transition layer (operator&, is_loading/is_saving) and beat Boost 1.1-2.8x in the chart's struct, map and string categories.
The project is already on C++20 (GCC 10+, Clang 13+, AppleClang 15+, MSVC VS 2019/2022) and builds with CMake 3.20+ or Bazel bzlmod.
Saving to or loading from std::ostringstream/istringstream or file streams, where per-call streambuf overhead dominates.
You care about debug builds. The README claims smaller debug symbols and a better debugging experience because of nodebug/always_inline wrappers, and 25% faster compiles, but gives no data.
when_not_to_use: Bulk arithmetic payloads (vector<double>, vector<uint8_t>, one large std::string): the repo's own numbers show parity with cereal and Boost.
Types with virtual bases or heavy polymorphism: PoDChild (virtual base) loads were about 7% slower than cereal (26.27 vs 24.64).
Portable-binary, JSON or XML archives: only BinaryArchive has the buffer. PortableBinaryArchive still calls sputn/sgetn for every value, and no benchmarks exist for the other archives.
You need top throughput: the author says it is 'by far not the fastest serialization library out there'. It keeps cereal's per-field stream model and only batches it.

Maturity or untrusted input matter: single maintainer, 34 stars, v0.9.1, no commits since 2025-06-25, no issue tracker activity. Container loads resize() to the size stored in the archive with no bound, so a hostile archive can force huge allocations.

integration.dependencies: None at runtime. It bundles rapidjson, rapidxml and base64 headers for the JSON/XML archives. Boost.Serialization is needed only for the optional comparison benchmark (SKIP_PERFORMANCE_COMPARISON=OFF).
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with concepts (C++17 is rejected with #error). CI covers GCC 10/12/14, Clang 13/15/16/18, AppleClang via Xcode 15.4/16.2, and MSVC on windows-2019/2025. Needs CMake 3.20+ or Bazel (bzlmod).
integration.platforms: Any platform with a C++20 compiler. CI runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows. BinaryArchive uses native endianness; PortableBinaryArchive handles endianness conversion.
integration.thread_safety: One archive must be used by one thread at a time. Running several archives in parallel is safe only with SER20_THREAD_SAFE=1, which puts mutexes around the global static registries. The CMake THREAD_SAFE option defaults to OFF and is only offered on UNIX.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — cereal code is source-compatible after renaming the cereal:: namespace and the CEREAL_* macros to SER20_*. JSON/XML class-version fields are written as 'ser20_class_version' instead of 'cereal_class_version'. Binary compatibility with cereal archives is not documented. Boost users get cereal's transition layer but must still port serialize(ar, version) signatures and registration macros.

gotchas: BinaryInputArchive reads ahead in 4 KiB sgetn chunks and never gives unused bytes back (the destructor is defaulted). After a load, the istream position can be past the end of the archive. Unlike cereal, which reads exactly the bytes it needs, you cannot interleave raw reads or run back-to-back archives on the same stream. On a pipe or socket streambuf, a small load may block until 4 KiB or EOF arrives.

BinaryOutputArchive holds data in a 4 KiB buffer until the end of each top-level ar(...) call or until destruction. Writes of 1 KiB or more bypass the buffer. Stream write or read failures throw ser20::Exception.

Version numbers disagree: the CMake project says 1.4.0 (used for the find_package SameMajorVersion check), version.hpp says 0.9.1 and MODULE.bazel says 0.9.0. version.hpp warns that compatibility is not guaranteed across versions.
The C++20 module file (module/ser20.cppm) is marked experimental and is not wired into the CMake build. The README's '15% smaller' and 'compile up to 25% faster' claims have no published data.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ser20 when you have cereal-style code, or need cereal features (polymorphic pointers, shared_ptr tracking, versioning, JSON/XML archives), and want a cheap speedup from a rename. For raw speed, bitsery and YAS report 3.5-10x wins over cereal and Boost in third-party suites, and Cista++ and struct_pack are different, much faster designs, but all of them are separate libraries with their own APIs.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's own sandbox/performance.cpp saves and loads the same data with Boost, cereal and ser20 binary archives to std::ostringstream/istringstream, averaged over 100 interleaved runs. The committed numbers show ser20 about 2.0x faster on save and 1.8x on load than cereal for vector<PoDStruct>, 2.1x/1.3x for map<string,PoDStruct>, and 1.85x/1.3x for the 'String' bar. That bar is most likely the vector<string> test, because a duplicate dict key overwrote the single-string entry, which was at parity. Against Boost the range is 1.1-2.8x, and bulk arithmetic vectors are at parity. Compiler, flags, CPU, library versions and the data size behind each bar are not stated, and no one has reproduced the results independently.
status_note: Stale single-maintainer project (v0.9.1, last commit 2025-06-25, 34 stars, no issues filed). It is BSD-3-Clause and small (two .cpp files plus cereal-derived headers), so it is easy to vendor. Upstream cereal (4.7k stars) is still being pushed to as of 2026-03.
